overview: Maize lethal necrosis is a serious disease caused by simultaneous infection involving maize chlorotic mottle virus and another compatible cereal virus.
symptoms: Chlorotic mottling that may progress to leaf necrosis
possible_causes: Combined viral infection, commonly maize chlorotic mottle virus with sugarcane mosaic virus or another compatible potyvirus
favorable_conditions: Continuous maize production can sustain disease pressure
spread: Insect vectors can transmit the component viruses
Movement of infected or contaminated seed and plant material can contribute to spread
prevention: Use tolerant or resistant varieties recommended locally
Control volunteer maize and relevant weed hosts
Follow local planting-time and vector-management guidance
management: Report suspected outbreaks to local agricultural authorities where MLN is regulated or emerging
Remove severely affected plants only according to local phytosanitary guidance
Do not rely on fungicides because MLN is viral
professional_help_message: Request field confirmation from an agricultural extension or plant-health authority when MLN is suspected.

overview: Maize streak disease is a viral disease transmitted primarily by leafhopper vectors.
symptoms: Narrow pale or yellow streaks running parallel to leaf veins
Severe early infection may cause stunting
Severe infection can contribute to poor yield
favorable_conditions: High activity of viruliferous leafhopper vectors
spread: Transmitted by leafhoppers after feeding on infected plants
The virus is not controlled by fungicides
prevention: Use resistant or tolerant varieties recommended locally
Manage volunteer cereals and relevant grass hosts
Use locally approved vector-management practices when justified
management: Confirm the disease because nutrient disorders and other viruses may also cause streaking
Seek local advice on integrated vector and crop management
professional_help_message: Request extension confirmation, especially when streaking and stunting occur across multiple plants.

overview: Northern leaf blight is a fungal maize disease that can reduce yield when susceptible crops are infected early and disease becomes severe.
symptoms: Long canoe-shaped lesions that become tan
Lesions often begin on lower leaves and may spread upward
spread: Spores develop on infected tissue and can move by wind
The pathogen can survive in maize debris
prevention: Rotate away from maize where appropriate
Manage infected residue using locally suitable practices
management: Scout fields and consider crop stage, hybrid susceptibility and weather
Use fungicides only when locally recommended and economically justified
professional_help_message: Seek agronomic advice if lesions reach upper leaves before or around flowering.

overview: Northern leaf spot is a fungal maize disease whose appearance can vary with pathogen race and maize genotype.
symptoms: Grayish-tan, narrow or oblong lesions with darker borders
Lesions may occur on leaves, sheaths or husks
spread: The pathogen produces spores under favorable conditions
prevention: Manage infected maize debris using locally suitable practices
management: Confirm the disease because symptoms can resemble other maize leaf diseases
Consider fungicide only under local professional guidance, particularly for susceptible seed-production lines
professional_help_message: Consult an agronomist if disease is widespread or the crop is a susceptible seed-production line.
